item.title: Transversal Gates and Magic State Distillation in an Optimally Synthesized Spin-Qubit Shuttling Bus
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Co-designed spin-qubit shuttling bus architecture enables all-to-all logical connectivity via transversal CNOT gates; symmetric shuttling reduces logical error rate by up to 60% compared to asymmetric shuttling at large code distances.

Grade 0.503 · 4.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “fault-tolerant logical gates and magic state distillation” · Pau Escofet, Andrii Semenov, Niall Murphy, Elena Blokhina, Carmen G. Almudéver, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcón

Figure

Logical error rate (LER) per transversal CNOT as a function of logical hop distance for code distances d=9,11,13. Solid lines show symmetric shuttling outperforming asymmetric shuttling (dashed lines) across all distances.

Asks

How can physical spin-qubit shuttling architectures be co-designed to support both optimized syndrome extraction and low-overhead transversal multi-qubit logical operations?

Before

1D shuttling-bus architecture optimized via Quantum Reverse Mapping only for single-logical-qubit syndrome extraction (Escofet 2026).

But

Circuit simulations under phenomenological dephasing and gate-noise parameters without full end-to-end magic state injection noise; based on surface code memory/tCNOT error rates combined via an additive error model.

Tools

Quantum Reverse Mapping · Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) · Circuit-level noise simulation · Rotated surface codes

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires not only reliable logical qubit storage, but also the ability to perform high-fidelity logical operations between error-corrected qubits at scale. While much of the existing literature focuses on optimizing syndrome extraction for a single logical qubit, the co-design of physical architectures that support both robust error correction and efficient logical computation remains an open challenge. In this work, we propose a multi-qubit spin-qubit shuttling bus architecture that addresses both requirements simultaneously. The architecture optimizes the physical qubit layout for syndrome extraction and supports transversal two-qubit logical gates between an arbitrary number of logical qubits, achieving all-to-all logical connectivity through coherent spin shuttling. We further propose an ancilla-sharing scheme that encodes multiple logical qubits within a single logical element, compressing the physical footprint of the processor and improving long-range gate fidelity. Extending the architecture from a one-dimensional bus to a two-dimensional grid of shuttling tracks reduces the inter-qubit distance, yielding consistent improvements in logical error. Finally, we apply the Quantum Reverse Mapping methodology at the logical level to optimize the layout of a 15-to-1 magic state distillation circuit, demonstrating how the transversal capabilities of the proposed architecture can be leveraged for universal fault-tolerant computation. Taken together, these results establish a principled co-design framework that bridges the physical, error-correction, and logical computation layers of the quantum stack, and demonstrate that spin-qubit shuttling architectures are a viable and flexible substrate for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation.

item.title: Need One Bell-pair Only (NOBOL) for Low-Overhead Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Realizes a logical CNOT between distant logical qubits encoded in arbitrary CSS codes using exactly one shared physical Bell pair state |Φ+⟩ and local gate operations with O(log⁡(τ)) depth, where τ is the logical operator support size.

Grade 0.502 · 4.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Sean Grzenda, Shahram Babaie, Chunming Qiao

Figure

Depth-optimal circuit execution for target logical qubit support |BXL|=8, achieving logarithmic depth via parallel hierarchical CNOT gates acting on ancilla q.

Asks

Can a remote logical CNOT across monolithic or distributed QPUs be implemented using only a single physical Bell pair instead of a logical Bell pair?

Before

Transversal remote gates, distributed lattice surgery, and gate/qubit teleportation require linear numbers of physical ancillae or logical Bell pairs scaling with code size.

But

Theoretical design; lacks quantitative numerical fault-tolerance thresholds or error rate simulations; reduced fault tolerance requires containment procedures (intermittent stabilization adding up to O(τBd) depth or repetition codes adding ancillae).

Tools

Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) codes · LOCC circuits · adaptive stabilizer tracking · repetition code encoding

Abstract

Fault-tolerant quantum computation fundamentally relies on encoding a logical qubit into a structured block of physical qubits, typically in the tens to hundreds. As a trade-off for improved fault-tolerance, logical gate operations will incur a linear overhead in terms of both the amount of time and quantum resources than before. For example, in monolithic quantum computing, performing a gate operation on two distant logical qubits will first require using a linear number of SWAP operations in order to move the logical qubits next to each other; while in distributed quantum computing, doing so will first require a linear number of ancilla qubits in order to form entanglement connections (or a logical Bell pair). In this paper, we focus on significantly reducing the overhead involved in logical CNOT operations, a fundamental primitive. We propose NOBOL, a novel approach that requires only one Bell pair to perform a logical CNOT operation on two distant qubits encoded in arbitrary CSS codes. More importantly, NOBOL only requires performing gate operations on the logical X or Z operator subsets of the logical qubits. For many CSS codes, such as the surface code, these subsets are significantly smaller than the size of the code itself. In this paper, we describe various circuit realizations of NOBOL, including a depth-optimal circuit with logarithmic depth in terms of the size of the logical operators. Finally, we propose effective methods to contain error propagation without incurring much additional overhead. Since NOBOL can be effectively applied to a wide range of quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes and, in addition, is agnostic to qubit modalities and effective for various architectures, including those based on either a monolithic QPU or distributed QPUs.

item.title: Optimal Fusion Strategies for Quantum Computation
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Optimal non-adaptive fusion strategy for a single-qubit stabilizer code is given by its largest non-trivial logical operator containing no non-identity stabilizer substring. A perfect fusion strategy exists whenever this operator has full weight, tolerating failure of all but one physical fusion.

Grade 0.477 · 3.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Kenneth Goodenough, Andrew Landahl, Joon Lee, Antonio Russo, Kevin Thompson

Figure

Schematic of single-qubit logical teleportation via physical pairwise fusions between code blocks L and LA, where failed fusions measure single-qubit Pauli observables and successful fusions perform Bell-state measurements.

Asks

Which quantum error-correcting codes and non-adaptive measurement bases admit perfect fusion strategies where only a single physical fusion must succeed?

But

Encodes a single qubit (k=1), non-adaptive strategies only, Pauli basis measurements (X, Y, or Z), noiseless/lossless channels with fusion failure as the sole error source.

Tools

stabilizer formalism · graph codes · local complementation · Paley-Zygmund inequality · random graph theory

Abstract

Logical fusions are important for a number of tasks in quantum information, such as quantum error correction and quantum repeaters. In the photonic setting one must contend with the fact that physical fusions are probabilistic (i.e.~the associated qubits are measured in product bases), which---depending on the failures and the associated bases---can lead to a failure on the logical level. The choice of failure basis of each qubit is known as a fusion strategy, and finding good fusion strategies is important for optimizing performance of fusion-based quantum computation. Here we provide a complete characterization when k=1 qubits are encoded, and in particular characterize those codes and fusion strategies such that all but one physical fusion can fail, i.e.~emphperfect fusion strategies. In doing so, we recover previously known perfect fusion strategies, and find perfect fusion strategies for quantum parity-check codes, answering an open question. We furthermore show that perfect fusion strategies are generic: random $[[n, 1, d]]$ graph codes admit a perfect fusion strategy with probability exponentially close to 1. Additionally we motivate the study of a new graph parameter, namely the maximum degree of a graph at a given vertex taken over all LC-equivalent graphs, by giving a new operationally meaningful interpretation of it.

item.title: Circuit-Level Loss Performance of FFCC and RHG Codes in a Compound Photon-Atom Quantum Architecture
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Under uniform circuit-level CZ loss in a compound photon-atom MBQC architecture, periodic RHG achieves the highest threshold at 2.75%. Reduced FFCC surpasses RHG only when excess loss on intermodule CZ connections is sufficiently large.

Grade 0.435 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Dana Ben Porath, Juval Bechar, Daniel Azses, Yaron Jarach

Figure

Circuit-level loss threshold as a function of excess intermodule loss q. RHG threshold starts highest at uniform loss (q=0) and drops below reduced FFCC as q increases.

Asks

Does reducing MBQC resource graph degree improve error-correction performance under an architecture-aware circuit-level loss model with delayed heralding and correlated bond loss?

Before

Under IID loss, the threshold was approximately 25% for RHG (Barrett & Stace 2010), 8.5% for FFCC, and 13.5% for reduced FFCC (Paesani & Brown 2023).

But

Simulations under periodic boundary conditions with photon-loss-only error model; atomic loss, dephasing, and photonic Pauli errors are neglected.

Tools

compound photon-atom unit cells · Stim detector error modeling · PyMatching MWPM decoding · bipartite and STAP generation schemes

Abstract

We compare the Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal (RHG) code, the Foliated Floquet Color Code (FFCC), and the reduced FFCC in a compound photon-atom architecture that directly generates measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) resources with near-deterministic photon-atom CZ gates. RHG serves as a natural benchmark, while the FFCC variants allow us to study whether reduced graph degree improves performance under an architecture-aware circuit-level loss model with delayed heralding and correlated bond-loss propagation. We construct two generation schemes compatible with the compound hardware and evaluate circuit-level thresholds under periodic boundary conditions. RHG achieves the highest circuit-level threshold, 2.75%, and its threshold falls below that of reduced FFCC only for large excess loss on intermodule CZ connections. RHG also achieves the lowest logical error rate in most resource-matched comparisons, but some low-loss windows favor reduced FFCC. Overall, we show that when the hardware supports the native gates and connectivity required for MBQC, the benefits of lower graph degree must be weighed against each code's intrinsic IID loss tolerance, generation-scheme details, and hardware-aware resource overhead.

item.title: An Entanglement-Assisted Stabilizer Framework for Distributed Sensing of Local Phases
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Joint entanglement-assisted stabilizer measurements allow remote ebit halves to estimate local phases while attaining the single-qubit quantum Fisher information and identifying X-type return errors, leaving the post-sensing state matching the original logical state up to a known Pauli operation.

Grade 0.425 · 2.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Huidan Zheng, Ilkwon Sohn, Jun Heo

Figure

Root-mean-square error of the estimated phase versus true phase for sample sizes M=20,100,500, showing convergence to the asymptotic 1/M shot-noise floor.

Asks

How can remote halves of entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting ebits act as distributed local-phase probes while preserving the encoded logical state for subsequent computation?

But

Assumes noiseless pre-shared ebits, noiseless Alice-side encoding and storage, ideal stabilizer measurements, and probe noise restricted to independent X errors occurring after phase acquisition.

Tools

entanglement-assisted stabilizer codes · graph codes · quantum Fisher information · remote-leaf-matched stabilizer graph topology

Abstract

Distributed quantum sensing requires spatially separated probes to acquire local parameters while maintaining compatibility with network-level quantum information processing. We develop an entanglement-assisted stabilizer framework based on the extended structure of entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting (EAQEC) codes, in which the remote halves of pre-shared ebits are used directly as local phase probes while the joint state simultaneously carries an encoded logical subsystem. Each remote probe acquires a local Z-axis phase and subsequently returns through an X-type noise channel. Within the extended EAQEC stabilizer structure, the stabilizer containing X_B_j provides phase-dependent measurement statistics, whereas its partner containing Z_B_j records the corresponding return-error syndrome. A graph-code formulation is introduced to make this structure explicit, together with an illustrative [[5,1,3;2]] construction. We further show that, conditioned on the joint sensing-and-syndrome measurement record, the post-sensing state differs from the original encoded state only by a known Pauli transformation, so that the logical information remains available for subsequent encoded operations. For the local-phase model considered here, the stabilizer readout attains the available quantum Fisher information, while the finite-shot estimator approaches the corresponding 1/√M scaling as the number of repetitions increases. The framework therefore provides a common entanglement-assisted stabilizer structure for distributed local-phase sensing, restricted return-error identification, and post-sensing logical-state retention, without relying on an intrinsic metrological enhancement from EAQEC itself.

item.title: Error accumulation in dissipative quantum circuits
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Average state fidelity decay in dissipative random circuits is universal and independent of dissipative Kraus rank r. Decay is completely governed by dissipation strength κ, qubit number L, and circuit depth T, while r affects only higher-moment fluctuations.

Grade 0.416 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Nadir Samos-Sáenz de Buruaga, Rodrigo M. C. Pereira, Karol Życzkowski, Sergey Denisov, Pedro Ribeiro

Figure

Mean fidelity as a function of circuit depth T for L=6 qubits. Data collapse onto theoretical predictions across varying dissipative Kraus ranks r, confirming rank independence.

Asks

How does the microscopic structure of local dissipative noise affect state fidelity decay in finite-depth random quantum circuits?

But

Requires random qubit permutation layers and Haar-random distributions for either the two-qubit unitaries or the dissipative Kraus operators.

Tools

diluted unitary channel model · Haar-averaged random matrix theory · many-body state fidelity in 4-copy Hilbert space

Code. https://github.com/nadir265/rqc_error_accumulation_diluted_circuits

Abstract

Present-day quantum processors are open systems in which dissipation and decoherence degrade the information carried by a quantum state as it propagates through a circuit. We study this degradation in dissipative random quantum circuits, modeling each two-qubit gate as a diluted unitary that interpolates between the intended unitary operation and a random dissipative quantum channel. Using the fidelity between the ideal and noisy output states as a diagnostic, we show that sufficiently random unitary gates or dissipative Kraus operators lead to a universal decay of the average fidelity. This decay is determined only by the dissipation strength, system size, and circuit depth, while microscopic details of the gates and noise, including the Kraus rank, appear only in subleading corrections to higher moments. We derive a closed-form expression for the average fidelity in terms of three physically meaningful error parameters, dissipation strength, coherent two-qubit gate-error strength, and connectivity-error probability. Finally, we identify the cases when dissipative effects can be reproduced by an unitary-noise model and when dissipation-induced decoherence remains distinguishable from coherent noise at the level of the average fidelity.

We study this degradation in dissipative random quantum circuits, modeling each two-qubit gate as a diluted unitary that interpolates between the intended unitary operation and a random dissipative quantum channel. Using the fidelity between the ideal and noisy output states as a diagnostic, we show that sufficiently random unitary gates or dissipative Kraus operators lead to a universal decay of the average fidelity. This decay is determined only by the dissipation strength, system size, and circuit depth, while microscopic details of the gates and noise, including the Kraus rank, appear only in subleading corrections to higher moments. We derive a closed-form expression for the average fidelity in terms of three physically meaningful error parameters, dissipation strength, coherent two-qubit gate-error strength, and connectivity-error probability. Finally, we identify the cases when dissipative effects can be reproduced by an unitary-noise model and when dissipation-induced decoherence remains distinguishable from coherent noise at the level of the average fidelity.

item.title: GadIR: A Spatial-Topology Preserving Compiler for Quantum Many-Body Systems Simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Preserving the spatial topology of physical many-body Hamiltonians via a Pauli-gadget intermediate representation reduces compilation overhead to 0.56 × (two-qubit gates on superconducting platforms), 0.87 × (infidelity on neutral-atom devices), 0.85 × (non-Clifford gates on fault-tolerant quantum computers), and 0.75 × (emitter-entangling operations in measurement-based quantum computing) relative to QuCLEAR.

Grade 0.390 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Xiangyu Ren, Yuexun Huang, Zhaohui Yang, Yuchen Zhu, Tsung-Wei Huang, Tsung-Yi Ho, Zhiding Liang, Antonio Barbalace

Figure

Normalized two-qubit gate counts across various many-body Hamiltonian benchmark models for compilation targeting IBM heavy-hexagon (CNOT) and Google square-grid (CZ) superconducting layouts.

Asks

How can quantum compilers preserve the spatial-topology information of many-body Hamiltonians to reduce hardware compilation overhead across diverse quantum architectures?

Before

QuCLEAR compiled Hamiltonians flattened as linear sequences of Pauli strings without hardware-independent topology-preserving intermediate representations.

But

Evaluated using single second-order Suzuki Trotter steps across four target architectures; structural Hamiltonian inputs set all term coefficients to 1.

Tools

GadIR intermediate representation · ZX-calculus and Pauli gadgets · Pauli gadget group reduction · Suzuki-Trotter decomposition

Code. https://github.com/xiyurain/GadIR

Abstract

Simulating quantum many-body systems has been one of the most important applications of quantum computation. For simulation, the Hamiltonian of a physical system is compiled into quantum programs with native instructions for quantum hardware. In previous works, the Hamiltonian is represented as Pauli strings, then compiled and optimized based on the quantum circuit model. Such representation paradigm neglects the spatial topology of original physical models, which is vital information to reducing the overhead of compiling many-body systems Hamiltonians. To address such neglect, we introduce a spatial-topology preserving compiler for quantum many-body simulation. Using Pauli gadgets as the representations of the Hamiltonian, we introduce our intermediate representation -- GadIR, to preserve the spatial-topology information of original physical models. Our compiler frontend performs the group reduction algorithm based on Pauli gadget model, which is a hardware-independent optimization. Our compiler backend performs trotterization and scheduling on Pauli gadgets, then synthesizes the Pauli gadgets into hardware-native quantum programs. We evaluate our compiler on all the canonical quantum many-body system models, while achieving a significant reduction on compilation overhead regarding four major quantum architectures. Overall, our spatial-topology preserving IR exploits the compilation optimization space for quantum many-body systems Hamiltonian.

item.title: Purification of photonic graph states
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Photonic CSS, GHZ, and arbitrary stabilizer graph states are purified using only linear optics and photon detectors via transversal type-I fusions, reaching per-round success probability up to 1/2. For 3-qubit (4-qubit) GHZ states under depolarization error pdep=0.05, two cascaded rounds raise fidelity from F≈0.86 (F≈0.81) to F=0.988 (F=0.981).

Grade 0.363 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Sparse-Graph Codes for Quantum Error Correction” · Matthias C. Löbl, Aliki A. Capatos, Ming Lai Chan, Peter Lodahl, Anders Søndberg Sørensen, Stefano Paesani

Figure

GHZ state fidelity plotted against qubit count (n=2 to 8) for depolarization noise pdep=0.05 across zero, one (bit- or phase-flip), and two cascaded purification rounds.

Asks

How can noisy photonic graph states generated by quantum emitters be purified without deterministic entangling gates?

Before

was 192 photons on average to produce a 3-qubit GHZ state probabilistically with all-linear optics; emitter-based generation with time-multiplexed two-round purification requires 96 photons.

But

Assumes error-free linear-optics circuits. First-order photon loss doubles for small loss rates pl under phase-flip purification.

Tools

transversal type-I fusion · polarizing beam splitters and photon-number-resolving detectors · quantum emitters in waveguides · stabilizer and CSS formalism

Abstract

Graph states constitute the main building block for quantum computing with photons. Quantum emitters with a hosted spin can deterministically generate photonic graph states, strongly lowering the overhead of multiplexing highly probabilistic linear-optics graph state generation. However, they generally suffer from various noise sources, resulting in reduced fidelities of the produced states. To mitigate this issue, we develop purification schemes for entangled photonic states. We first develop purification schemes to purify arbitrary photonic GHZ and other CSS states, which we generalize to all photonic graph states and stabilizer states. The proposed purification schemes have a high success probability of up to 1/2 and require only linear optics and photon detectors. We optimize cascaded purification schemes for various graph states, taking into account phenomenological Pauli errors or physical noise in time-bin-encoded graph state generation with quantum emitters.
